question.passageWithMarkers: The structure of glass is, frankly, a bit of a mess. Clear and perfect __(A) as__ it might appear to our eyes, down at the molecular level, glass looks more like a random ball-pit of atoms. The technical term for this mess depends on who you're asking: for some scientists it is an "amorphous solid," for others a "supercooled liquid." In theory it's both liquid and solid, though, given the way it behaves, in practice it's really the latter. In fact, at room temperature glass never __(B) behaves__ as a liquid, even an imperceptibly viscous one, even over long periods of time (though it can "sweat" if you don't add enough lime to the mix). Those misshapen sheets of glass you sometimes see in old stained-glass windows, thicker at the bottom than the top, __(C) is__ generally not that way because the glass is slowly sinking over time. __(D) Unless__ the church has endured temperatures of more than 400˚C, the chances are they are uneven because that's the way they were blown and solidified in the first place. Flat glass was only developed in the nineteenth century and we had to wait until the middle of the twentieth century for truly flat, thin sheets of glass. The paradox is __(E) that__, despite it being one of the very oldest human-made substances, scientists still struggle to comprehend why glass behaves the way it does. Glass seems to obey most molecular laws. As one glassmaker put it, glass is not a material; it's a state.

question.passageWithMarkers: To minimize building costs and maximize revenues, skyscrapers generally take the shape of squares or rectangles. These are not particularly aerodynamic shapes, and this results in a wind phenomenon called "vortex shedding." As wind meets a rectangular skyscraper it pushes on the flat face of the building before __(A) flowing__ around its sides, where eventually it __(B) separates__ from the face of the structure. The difference in pressures on the front and back faces of the building gives rise to vortices, or __(C) spinning__ currents of wind, that flow downstream from the building. The vortices pull and push the building in a direction __(D) perpendicularly__ to the wind at frequencies that can become dangerously self-sustaining. To minimize vortex shedding, skyscraper designers do everything in their powers to confuse the wind. __(E) Orienting__ the building so that the longer face of the structure is parallel with prevailing winds can help. Chopping or rounding off corners of a building can likewise make it more aerodynamic. Roughing up the corners of the building through the careful placement of balconies or stepped corners can help by disturbing or delaying the formation of strong vortices.

question.passageWithMarkers: The structure of glass __(A) is__, frankly, a bit of a mess. Clear and perfect as it might appear to our eyes, down at the molecular level, glass looks more like a random ball-pit of atoms. The technical term for this mess depends on who you're asking: for some scientists it is an "amorphous solid," for others a "supercooled liquid." In theory it's both liquid and solid, though, given the way it behaves, in practice it's really the latter. In fact, at room temperature glass never __(B) behaves__ as a liquid, even an imperceptibly viscous one, even over long periods of time (though it can "sweat" if you don't add enough lime to the mix). Those misshapen sheets of glass you sometimes see in old stained-glass windows, thicker at the bottom than the top, are generally not that way because the glass is slowly sinking over time. Unless the church __(C) has endured__ temperatures of more than 400˚C, the chances are they are uneven because that's the way they were blown and solidified in the first place. Flat glass was only developed in the nineteenth century and we had to wait until the middle of the twentieth century for __(D) truly__ flat, thin sheets of glass. The paradox is that, despite it being one of the very oldest human-made substances, scientists still struggle __(E) comprehending__ why glass behaves the way it does. Glass seems to obey most molecular laws. As one glassmaker put it, glass is not a material; it's a state.

In certain languages, the same word can mean "red" or simply "colored," depending on the context, such as coloratus in classical Latin or colorado in modern Castilian.
